newsitem.title: USA: Boeing sees healthy demand for aircraft.
newsitem.headline: Boeing sees healthy demand for aircraft.

text.p: Boeing Co. Tuesday gave an upbeat forecast of world aircraft orders, predicting airlines will add 16,160 new jets worth $1.1 trillion over the next 20 years, paced by growth in the Asia-Pacific market.

The world's largest commercial aircraft maker said it expects the global fleet to be 23,600 passenger and cargo planes in the year 2016. At the end of 1996, the jetliner fleet totalled 11,500. Boeing made 7,000 of those aircraft, giving it 61 percent of the market.
The Seattle-based company projected that 4,060 aircraft currently flying would be retired by 2016.
Bruce Dennis, vice president of marketing for Boeing Commercial Airplane Group, said Boeing hopes to boost its share to 67 percent of all orders.
To meet the demand, Boeing plans to boost monthly production to a record 40 aircraft a month in the fourth quarter from 22.5 in the 1996 fourth quarter, Dennis told a news conference.
Boeing projected that air travel would grow 4.9 percent a year between now and 2016.
That growth is slightly lower than the 5.1 percent Boeing predicted a year-ago due to a maturing U.S. market and lower estimates for the Asia-Pacific region.

Annual traffic growth is expected to be fastest in Asia-Pacific, with annual projected growth of 6.6 percent. The U.S. market will grow by 3.1 percent a year, while European growth was pegged at 4.4 percent annually, Boeing said.
"The industry continues on the upswing," Dennis said.

Of the predicted $1.1 trillion of new orders, one-third of the new business is expected to come from the Asia-Pacific region. North America will account for 28 percent, Europe 26 percent and the rest of the world 13 percent.
Dennis told reporters that Boeing's market research indicated that the market for aircraft larger than 500 seats was only 480 aircraft over the next 20 years.
"The market demand just isn't there right now for an airplane larger than our 747 jumbo jet," he said.
Boeing's decision not to develop larger aircraft was based on low customer demand, coupled with the high investment that would be needed.

Dennis said customers, particularly in Asia and the Pacific Rim, were more interested in a "stretch" version of the smaller 777 aircraft that would allow airlines to offer more frequent flights over long-haul routes.
"However, we continue to study the market and, if the potential develops for that size of airplane, we'll be ready with an excellent design," he said.

Airbus Industrie, the European consortium, is the only manufacturer pressing ahead with plans to develop a "super jumbojet." McDonnell Douglas Corp. also considered making a larger plane before scrapping those plans and agreeing to merge with Boeing.

Boeing projected that single-aisle airplanes, the size of the Boeing 737 and 757, would account for 43 percent of the dollars invested in the world's fleet by 2016 and would account for 70 percent of the total fleet.

The fastest-growing market segment will be for twin-aisle airplanes, such as the Boeing 767 and 777, which are expected to account for 39 percent of the value of the new orders, while 747 or larger airplanes would get 18 percent of the dollars invested.
Boeing's stock lost $1.875 to $100.25 in consolidated New York Stock Exchange trading.
